definition: Seeming reasonable and believable enough that it could be true, even if not proven.
example: Her excuse about a flat bike tire sounded plausible, so the coach let her join practice late.
nuance: Plausible means an idea could believably be true; probable means it is more likely true than not. A plausible claim may still turn out false.
prompt: Scientists are trying to explain why the fish population in a mountain lake suddenly dropped.
options: Warmer water holding less oxygen offered a plausible explanation for the sudden decline.
The researchers found it plausible to collect water samples every morning before breakfast.
The idea that the fish swam off to the ocean was plausible, even though the lake has no outlet.
The volunteers who counted the fish earned a plausible round of applause at the meeting.
reasons: A cause that fits the known facts and could reasonably be true is exactly what the word describes.
This confuses the word with feasible; it describes believable claims, not tasks that can be managed.
A theory the facts rule out is far-fetched, which is the opposite of believable.
The word only looks like applause; in modern English it does not mean deserving praise.

practice.prompt: A novelist needs readers to accept why her main character misses an important train.
options: The writer printed the draft in a plausible font so the editor could read it easily.
Her editor called the chapter plausible simply because it was exactly twenty pages long.
Oversleeping after a double shift gave the character a plausible reason to miss the train.
Readers found it plausible that a talking cloud lifted her off the platform and flew her home.
reasons: How easy a typeface is to read has nothing to do with whether something is believable.
Page count says nothing about whether events in the story seem true to life.
An ordinary, realistic cause is one readers can easily believe.
A wildly impossible event in a realistic story strains belief instead of earning it.
